passages.t: A paralyzed man forgiven and healed
passages.happening:
Jesus is back in Capernaum, and so many people pack into the house that no one else can get near the door. Four men arrive carrying a friend who cannot walk. They climb onto the roof, dig an opening, and lower him on his mat right in front of Jesus.

Jesus sees their faith and says something nobody expects: “Son, your sins are forgiven.” Some scribes sitting there are shocked. They think, “Who can forgive sins but God alone?” Jesus knows what they are thinking. To show that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins, he tells the man to get up, pick up his mat, and go home. The man does, in front of everyone. The crowd says, “We have never seen anything like this!”
passages.hearers:
Most houses in a town like Capernaum were small, built of the dark local stone, around a shared courtyard. Roofs were flat, made of wooden beams covered with branches and packed earth, and people reached them by an outside stair. Mark's Greek says the friends ‘dug through’ the roof. Luke, telling the same story, speaks of tiles (Luke 5:19). Either way, it was noisy, dusty, and rude. Dirt would have been falling on the people inside.

Many people in Jesus' day assumed that sickness was linked to sin. The man's friends brought him for healing, not forgiveness. Jesus starts with the deeper need.

The scribes are not being petty. They are right that only God can forgive sins against God. Their logic is sound. That is exactly what makes Jesus' words so startling. Either he is claiming what belongs to God, or he is speaking wrongly about God, which is what blasphemy means.
passages.ot:
God says through Isaiah, “I, yes I, am He who blots out your transgressions for My own sake” (Isaiah 43:25). In Israel, forgiveness came from God, usually through the priests and the sacrifices at the temple. Jesus gives it in a house in Galilee, with a word.

This is the first time Jesus calls himself the Son of Man in Mark. The title comes from Daniel 7:13-14, where “One like the Son of Man” comes with the clouds of heaven and is given “dominion, glory, and kingship.” Jesus says that figure's authority is already at work ‘on earth’.
passages.hard: Does Jesus claim to be God here, or does he only announce God's forgiveness, as a prophet might? Mark lets the scribes say the question out loud: “Who can forgive sins but God alone?” Jesus does not correct them. Instead he heals the man as proof that his word has weight. Mark wants the reader to feel the force of the scribes' question and to follow it to its end. The notes below take this question further.
passages.asks: The four friends could not heal the man, but they could carry him, and they would not let a crowd or a roof stop them. Jesus saw ‘their faith’. Ask who you are carrying to Jesus. And ask whether you, like the man on the mat, have come for a smaller gift than the one he wants to give.

passages.t: Levi called; Jesus eats with sinners
passages.happening: Jesus walks by the lake and sees a man named Levi sitting at his tax booth. He says, “Follow Me,” and Levi gets up and follows. Soon Jesus is eating at Levi's house with a crowd of tax collectors and ‘sinners’. Some scribes who belong to the Pharisees ask his disciples why he eats with people like that. Jesus answers, “It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick. I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.”
passages.hearers:
Capernaum sat near the border between the lands of Herod Antipas and those of his brother Philip, on a road used by traders. Levi was most likely a toll collector, taking customs on goods for Herod Antipas. Tax collectors usually worked for a ruler who answered to Rome, and they had a reputation for taking more than was owed. Many Jews saw them as traitors who grew rich off their neighbours.

‘Sinners’ did not mean everyone, though everyone sins. It meant people known for living outside God's law: people whose work or way of life put them beyond respectable company.

In that world, eating together meant acceptance. To share a table was to say, ‘You are one of us.’ The Pharisees were a group devoted to keeping God's law carefully, including rules about food and purity at meals. To them, a teacher who ate with such people seemed to approve of how they lived.
passages.ot: The prophets often spoke of God as a healer of his people and a shepherd who goes after the lost (Ezekiel 34:16). Jesus' picture of the doctor fits that hope. He has come for the people who know they are sick.
passages.hard: Does Jesus mean that some people are righteous and do not need him? No. His words have a sharp edge. Those who think they are healthy will not call a doctor. The Pharisees' problem is not that they are too good, but that they do not see their own need.
passages.asks: Jesus called Levi from his booth, a place of money and compromise, with two words. He did not first ask him to clean up his life. Ask who you would keep away from your table. Then ask whether you have ever been the one who needed someone to sit with you.

passages.t: The question about fasting: bridegroom, patch, and wineskins
passages.happening: People notice that John the Baptist's followers and the Pharisees fast, going without food for a time to pray, but Jesus' disciples do not. They ask why. Jesus answers with a picture: wedding guests do not fast while the bridegroom is with them. A day will come when the bridegroom is taken away, and then they will fast. He adds two more pictures: no one sews a new, unshrunk patch on an old coat, and no one pours new wine into old wineskins.
passages.hearers:
The law of Moses commanded only one fast a year, on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:29). But many devout Jews fasted more often. In Luke, a Pharisee says, “I fast twice a week” (Luke 18:12). Fasting was a sign of serious faith, and of mourning and longing for God to act.

A wedding in a Jewish village was a feast that could last for days. Fasting at a wedding would have been rude, even absurd.

The other two pictures come from daily life. New cloth shrinks the first time it is washed, so a new patch on an old coat pulls and tears it. Wine was kept in skins made of leather. New wine is still fermenting and gives off gas, so it stretches its container. A fresh skin can stretch with it. An old skin is dry and stiff, and it bursts.
passages.ot: In the Old Testament, God is pictured as the husband of his people: “as a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, so your God will rejoice over you” (Isaiah 62:5; see also Hosea 2:19). When Jesus calls himself the bridegroom, he takes up a picture the prophets used of God.
passages.hard: ‘The bridegroom will be taken from them’ is the first hint in Mark that Jesus will die. It comes very early, before anyone has plotted against him. The joy of the wedding already has a shadow over it.
passages.asks: Jesus is not against fasting. He says his followers will fast. He is against religious habits that miss what God is doing now. Ask whether your faith has room for something new from God, or whether it has gone stiff like an old skin.

passages.happening: On a Sabbath, Jesus and his disciples walk through fields of grain. As they go, the disciples pick some heads of grain. Pharisees object that this is against the law on the Sabbath. Jesus reminds them of a story about David: when David and his men were hungry, he went into the house of God and ate the holy bread that only priests were allowed to eat. Then he says, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. Therefore, the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath.”
passages.hearers:
The problem is not that the disciples took someone else's grain. The law allowed a hungry traveller to pick grain by hand from a neighbour's field, though not to bring a sickle (Deuteronomy 23:25). The problem is the day.

The Sabbath, the seventh day, was a gift and a sign of Israel's covenant with God. No work was to be done (Exodus 20:8-10), and the law named harvest time in particular (Exodus 34:21). Jewish teachers worked hard to define what counted as work, so that people could keep the command faithfully. Later, around AD 200, these rulings were written down in a collection called the Mishnah. It lists thirty-nine kinds of work, and reaping and threshing are among them. Picking grain and rubbing it in the hand looked like a small harvest.

The Pharisees were not monsters. They loved the Sabbath and wanted to protect it. That is what makes the clash serious.
passages.ot:
The story Jesus tells is in 1 Samuel 21:1-6. David, on the run from King Saul, came to the priest at Nob and asked for bread. The only bread there was the bread of the Presence, twelve loaves set out before God each week, which the law gave to the priests alone to eat (Leviticus 24:5-9). The priest gave it to David. Jesus' point is that human need, and David's mission, came before the rule about the bread.

The Sabbath itself goes back to creation, when God rested on the seventh day (Genesis 2:3). In Deuteronomy it is also a day of rest for servants, because Israel had been slaves in Egypt (Deuteronomy 5:14-15). It was always meant as mercy.
passages.hard: Jesus says David did this “During the high priesthood of Abiathar,” but 1 Samuel 21 names the priest as Ahimelech. Abiathar was Ahimelech's son, who escaped Saul's slaughter of the priests and became David's priest (1 Samuel 22:20). Matthew and Luke, telling the same story, leave the name out. Several answers have been offered. The Greek phrase can mean ‘in the time of Abiathar’, and Abiathar was the well known priest of David's day. Or it may mean ‘in the passage about Abiathar’, the way Mark 12:26 says ‘about the bush’ for the story of Moses and the burning bush. Others think it is a slip, by Mark or by an early copyist. The chapter's notes below lay out the views.
passages.asks: Rules can be good gifts that we turn into burdens. Jesus does not throw out the Sabbath. He claims to be its Lord, and he says it was made to serve people. Ask whether your religious habits are a gift that gives you rest, or a load you carry to prove yourself.
